name: Three-cueing (MSV): guess words from meaning, structure, and visual cues
sor_correction: Skilled readers identify words by processing the letters and sounds, not by guessing from context. Teach children to decode by mapping letters to sounds and blending.

name: Children should guess unknown words from the pictures
cue_patterns: use the pictures to figure out
sor_correction: Pictures can support meaning and vocabulary, but beginners should work out words by decoding the print, so the habit of guessing does not replace sounding out.

name: Children learn to read best through their own learning style (visual, auditory, kinesthetic)
sor_correction: Matching reading instruction to a child's preferred learning style has not been shown to improve outcomes. Explicit, systematic instruction helps all beginners, and multisensory activities can be used as engagement tools.

name: Beginning readers should only read leveled texts matched to a reading level
sor_correction: Beginners need practice with text that matches the phonics they have been taught (decodable text). Leveled text often relies on pictures and repeated patterns that invite guessing.

name: Children will learn to read naturally if they are surrounded by books
sor_correction: Learning to speak is natural; learning to read print is not. Most children need explicit, systematic teaching of how letters represent sounds. Rich book experiences still build vocabulary and knowledge.

name: Dyslexia means seeing letters or words backwards
sor_correction: Dyslexia is mainly a difficulty with phonological processing and word reading, not a visual problem. Reversals are common in all beginners and are not a reliable sign.
